title: We found a bug in Go's ARM64 compiler
dot: digraph G{rankdir=TB;node[shape=box, style=filled, fillcolor=lightgrey, fontname=Arial];edge[fontname=Arial];subgraph cluster_0{label="Investigating a strange panic";node[style=none];img1[shape=none, image="https://cf-assets.www.cloudflare.com/zkvhlag99gkb/1zaMttyutjMsqHUuEpCss3/8b7eb27d92e5fc53f6541d04fe0b778f/Bug_Bounty.png", label=""];text1[label="Every second, 84 million HTTP requests are hitting Cloudflare across our fleet of data centers in 330 cities. It means that even the rarest of bugs can show up frequently. In fact, it was our scale that recently led us to discover a bug in Go's arm64 compiler which causes a race condition in the generated code."];img2[shape=none, image="https://cf-assets.www.cloudflare.com/zkvhlag99gkb/7ohMD2ph3I9l7lbZQWZ4xl/243e679d8293565fc6a55a670c9f3583/BLOG-2906_2.png", label=""];text2[label="When we first saw this bug we saw that the fatal errors correlated with recovered panics. These were caused by some old code which used panic/recover as error handling."];text3[label="1. All of the fatal panics happen within stack unwinding.2. We correlated an increased volume of recovered panics with these fatal panics.3. Recovering a panic unwinds goroutine stacks to call deferred functions.4. A related Go issue (#73259) reported an arm64 stack unwinding crash.5. Let’s stop using panic/recover for error handling and wait out the upstream fix?"];text4[label="So we did that and watched as fatal panics stopped occurring as the release rolled out. Fatal panics gone, our theoretical mitigation seemed to work, and this was no longer our problem. We subscribed to the upstream issue so we could update when it was resolved and put it out of our minds."];text5[label="But, this turned out to be a much stranger bug than expected. Putting it out of our minds was premature as the same class of fatal panics came back at a much higher rate. A month later, we were seeing up to 30 daily fatal panics with no real discernible cause; while that might account for only one machine a day in less than 10% of our data centers, we found it concerning that we didn’t understand the cause."];}subgraph cluster_1{label="Fatal Error and Segmentation Fault";node[style=none];img3[shape=none, image="https://cf-assets.www.cloudflare.com/zkvhlag99gkb/5LKOBC6lQzuKvwy0vyEfk2/054c9aaedc14d155294a682f7de3a610/BLOG-2906_3.png", label=""];text6[label="Now we could observe some clear patterns. Both errors occur when unwinding the stack in (*unwinder).next. In one case we saw an intentional[fatal error](https://github.com/golang/go/blob/b3251514531123d7fd007682389bce7428d159a0/src/runtime/traceback.go#L566) as the runtime identified that unwinding could not complete and the stack was in a bad state. In the other case there was a direct memory access error that happened while trying to unwind the stack. The segfault was discussed in the [GitHub issue](https://github.com/golang/go/issues/73259#issuecomment-2786818812) and a Go engineer identified it as dereference of a go scheduler struct, [m](https://github.com/golang/go/blob/924fe98902cdebf20825ab5d1e4edfc0fed2966f/src/runtime/runtime2.go#L536), when[unwinding](https://github.com/golang/go/blob/b3251514531123d7fd007682389bce7428d159a0/src/runtime/traceback.go#L458)."];text7[label="A review of Go scheduler structs"];text8[label="Go uses a lightweight userspace scheduler to manage concurrency. Many goroutines are scheduled on a smaller number of kernel threads – this is often referred to as M:N scheduling. Any individual goroutine can be scheduled on any kernel thread. The scheduler has three core types – [`g`](https://github.com/golang/go/blob/924fe98902cdebf20825ab5d1e4edfc0fed2966f/src/runtime/runtime2.go#L394) (the goroutine), [`m`](https://github.com/golang/go/blob/924fe98902cdebf20825ab5d1e4edfc0fed2966f/src/runtime/runtime2.go#L536) (the kernel thread, or “machine”), and [`p`](https://github.com/golang/go/blob/924fe98902cdebf20825ab5d1e4edfc0fed2966f/src/runtime/runtime2.go#L644) (the physical execution context, or “processor”). For a goroutine to be scheduled a free `m` must acquire a free `p`, which will execute a g. Each `g` contains a field for its m if it is currently running, otherwise it will be **nil**. This is all the context needed for this post but the [go runtime docs](https://github.com/golang/go/blob/master/src/runtime/HACKING.md#gs-ms-ps) explore this more comprehensively."];}subgraph cluster_2{label="What's (async) preemption?";node[style=none];text9[label="In the prehistoric era of Go (<=1.13) the runtime was cooperatively scheduled. A goroutine would run until it decided it was ready to yield to the scheduler – usually due to explicit calls to `runtime.Gosched()` or injected yield points at function calls/IO operations. Since[Go 1.14](https://go.dev/doc/go1.14#runtime) the runtime instead does async preemption. The Go runtime has a thread `sysmon` which tracks the runtime of goroutines and will preempt any that run for longer than 10ms (at time of writing). It does this by sending `SIGURG` to the OS thread and in the signal handler will modify the program counter and stack to mimic a call to `asyncPreempt`."];text10[label="At this point we had two broad theories:*   This is a Go Netlink bug – likely due to `unsafe.Pointer` usage which invoked undefined behavior but is only actually broken on arm64*   This is a Go runtime bug and we're only triggering it in `NetlinkSocket.Receive` for some reason"];}subgraph cluster_3{label="Building a minimal reproducer";node[style=none];text11[label="This function ends up with a stack frame slightly larger than can be represented in 16 bits, and so on arm64 the Go compiler will split the stack pointer adjustment into two opcodes. If the runtime preempts between these opcodes then the stack unwinder will read an invalid stack pointer and crash."];text12[label="A single-instruction race condition window"];}img1->text1;text1->img2;img2->text2;text2->text3;text3->text4;text4->text5;text5->img3;img3->text6;text6->text7;text7->text8;text8->text9;text9->text10;text10->text11;text11->text12;}
